sections.label: The opening
sections.line: We teach programming the way Lockhart says we teach maths: upside down. Explorer coding starts at the right end.
sections.para: Lockhart wrote that we could not design a better system for destroying curiosity about maths. Programming is usually taught the same way, concepts before purpose. What hooks a programmer is control, in a short loop, which BASIC, Visual Basic, spreadsheets, Scratch and Code Club all had. Explorer coding starts there, and people will read more code, not less.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Seven lines: Lockhart, programming taught the same way, the hook, the loop, Excel, explorer coding, communication.
sections.para: Maths is taught as if to make people hate it, and so is programming: concepts first, often nothing useful. What hooks a programmer is control in a short loop, which the good tools had. Taught badly, people program in Excel instead. Explorer coding, by voice, starts at the right end, and coding is communication.

sections.label: Lockhart, on maths
sections.line: Paul Lockhart's A Mathematician's Lament, quoted in the book: maths taught to destroy curiosity.
sections.para: The essay of 2002 opens with a musician's nightmare of music taught like maths, and says Lockhart could not design a better mechanism for destroying a child's curiosity and love of pattern-making than current maths education. For him mathematics is an art. The memo misnamed him again; it is Paul Lockhart.

sections.label: We do the same with programming
sections.line: Programming is usually taught upside down: concepts that make no sense yet, before any purpose.
sections.para: Functions, types and structures arrive before anything you want them for. Even at university, with statistics software like SPSS, important concepts come at the wrong moment. People dislike it because nothing has made it make sense. Lockhart's point, moved from maths to code.

sections.label: What hooks a programmer
sections.line: The hook is control: going from a thought to something that works, in a short loop.
sections.para: I learned on a ZX Spectrum, then an Amiga and an x86, meeting each concept when a problem needed it. The REPL, read, evaluate, print, loop, is what makes it rewarding: solving little puzzles all the time, and building tools you use yourself.

sections.label: The tools that got the loop right
sections.line: The tools that taught well had a short loop: Scratch, Code Club, Visual Basic, the spreadsheet.
sections.para: Scratch, a block-based visual language from the MIT Media Lab, released in 2007; Code Club's volunteer-run after-school clubs, planned from April 2012 and part of the Raspberry Pi Foundation since 2015; Visual Basic from 1991, with drag-and-drop forms; and the spreadsheet, where changing a cell shows the result.

sections.label: The irony: back to Excel
sections.line: The irony: taught programming with nothing to build, people go back to Excel and program there.
sections.para: Microsoft's researchers call Excel the world's most widely used programming language, and since LAMBDA in January 2021, Turing-complete. The book reads the spreadsheet's persistence as software failing its users, since there they control the shape of the thing. People program wherever the loop is short and the result is theirs.

sections.label: Explorer coding starts at the right end
sections.line: Explorer coding starts at the right end: what you want, by voice, and seeing it work.
sections.para: It is why explorer coding, often called vibe coding, is powerful, with people now coding by voice. Founders who have explored for a while are ready for variables, procedures, methods and classes, and meet them in the code the agent writes, because a problem needs them.

sections.label: Coding is communication
sections.line: Coding is communication with a computer; the primitives stay, and people will read more code.
sections.para: A programming language is an abstraction layer for speaking to a computer, each with its sweet spot. The way in may become more visual or spoken, but the core primitives remain, and more people will understand them because they arrived from something they wanted to do.

sections.label: What I hope changes
sections.line: The conversational way in is crude but improving, and may bring many more people into building.
sections.para: The connection between what you do and what happens is now much more real. I hope more people discover development: solving little problems all the time and building tools they use, the experience the classroom often took away.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Not every course is like this; the experiences are mine; explorer coding is not a curriculum.
sections.para: Many teachers teach programming well; the pattern is common, not universal. The experiences are mine and my children's, not a study. Explorer coding is a way in, and the concepts still have to be learned. Lockhart wrote about maths; applying it to programming is my argument.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: A voice memo, the book's chapters, Lockhart's essay, Microsoft on LAMBDA, Code Club and Wikipedia.
sections.para: A voice memo of 21 October 2026, related to three chapters of the book; Paul Lockhart's essay; Microsoft Research on LAMBDA, January 2021; Code Club's 2015 announcement; Wikipedia on Scratch and Visual Basic; and related newsroom articles on explorer coding and citizen developers.
